SLAYER STATUTE — DISQUALIFICATION FROM INHERITING INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Jordan Lee is reviewing this information sheet in connection with the estate of Pat Morgan. This sheet explains, on a general informational basis only, California's "slayer statute" doctrine under Probate Code Part 7 (commencing with Section 250) — the rule that disqualifies a person who feloniously and intentionally kills a decedent from inheriting or otherwise benefiting from that decedent's estate — as it applies broadly to a will, a trust, intestate succession, a joint tenancy interest, and other property or benefits passing by reason of a decedent's death. It does not separately restate the corpus's existing, life-insurance-specific treatment of Prob. Code § 252 found in the Life Insurance Beneficiary Designation Information Sheet; a reader concerned with a named life insurance beneficiary should consult that document instead. This sheet states general facts about how California's slayer statute works. It is not, and does not attempt to be, a finding, determination, accusation, or admission that Pat Morgan died as a result of a felonious and intentional killing, or that any particular person committed one; it does not identify, name, or make any claim about any individual, and it does not advise Jordan Lee or anyone else on what to do about any actual situation.

WHAT THE SLAYER STATUTE DISQUALIFIES A KILLER FROM
Prob. Code § 250(a) states the core rule broadly: a person who feloniously and intentionally kills the decedent — that is, kills Pat Morgan — is not entitled to five categories of property, interest, or benefit. The first is any property, interest, or benefit under a will of the decedent or a trust created by or for the decedent's benefit or in which the decedent has an interest, which reaches not only outright gifts but also a general or special power of appointment the will or trust confers on the killer and any nomination of the killer as executor, trustee, guardian, conservator, or custodian. The second is any property passing by intestate succession. The third is the decedent's quasi-community property the killer would otherwise acquire under Prob. Code § 101 or § 102 on the decedent's death. The fourth is any property under Division 5 (commencing with Section 5000) — California's nonprobate-transfers division, which includes the payable-on-death and beneficiary-designation mechanisms addressed elsewhere in this corpus (including a life insurance policy's nonprobate transfer provision, separately covered by the Life Insurance Beneficiary Designation Information Sheet's own § 252 and § 250(a)(4) clause). The fifth is any property under Division 6, Part 3 (commencing with Section 6500) — the family-protection provisions governing a surviving spouse's or minor children's temporary possession of the family dwelling and certain exempt property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A person who feloniously and intentionally kills the decedent is not entitled to any of the following: (1) Any property, interest, or benefit under a will of the decedent, or a trust created by or for the benefit of the decedent or in which the decedent has an interest, including any general or special power of appointment conferred by the will or trust on the killer and any nomination of the killer as executor, trustee, guardian, or conservator or custodian made by the will or trust. (2) Any property of the decedent by intestate succession. (3) Any of the decedent’s quasi-community property the killer would otherwise acquire under Section 101 or 102 upon the death of the decedent. (4) Any property of the decedent under Division 5 (commencing with Section 5000). (5) Any property of the decedent under Part 3 (commencing with Section 6500) of Division 6."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 250(a), California Probate Code, general slayer statute — categories of disqualified property, interests, and benefits (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=250.)
  Known gap: This quotes subdivision (a) of a single statutory section, Prob. Code § 250; it was fetched twice independently (two distinct browser User-Agent strings against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) and the retrieved text was identical both times. Paragraph (a)(4)'s cross-reference to Division 5 is the same statutory text already quoted in this corpus's separate lifeinsbene_slayer_statute clause for the life-insurance-specific context — it is not an independent source, and this clause does not re-describe what Division 5 or §§ 101–102 (quasi-community property) themselves provide beyond what § 250(a) states about them. This clause does not determine, and is not evidence of, whether any actual killing occurred or was felonious and intentional; that question, and how it is established, is addressed separately (see § 254, below).

THE STATUTORY MECHANISM: TREATED AS HAVING PREDECEASED THE DECEDENT
Prob. Code § 250(b) specifies how disqualified property is redirected, rather than simply leaving it undistributed. For the will-or-trust interests described in § 250(a)(1), the property or benefit passes as if the killer had predeceased the decedent, and the statute expressly states that Prob. Code § 21110 (the anti-lapse statute governing what happens when a beneficiary predeceases a testator) does not apply to that substitution. The same predecease treatment applies to a property interest or benefit that passes to the killer under a power of appointment by reason of the decedent's death, with § 250(b)(2) similarly stating that Prob. Code § 673 does not apply. And any nomination of the killer as executor, trustee, guardian, conservator, or custodian that would otherwise become effective on the decedent's death is likewise interpreted as if the killer had predeceased the decedent — meaning an alternate or successor named in the governing instrument, rather than the disqualified killer, takes the nominated role.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(b) In the cases covered by subdivision (a): (1) The property interest or benefit referred to in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) passes as if the killer had predeceased the decedent and Section 21110 does not apply. (2) Any property interest or benefit referred to in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) which passes under a power of appointment and by reason of the death of the decedent passes as if the killer had predeceased the decedent, and Section 673 does not apply. (3) Any nomination in a will or trust of the killer as executor, trustee, guardian, conservator, or custodian which becomes effective as a result of the death of the decedent shall be interpreted as if the killer had predeceased the decedent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 250(b), California Probate Code, general slayer statute — predecease mechanism for redirecting disqualified property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=250.)
  Known gap: This quotes subdivision (b) of the same statutory section already quoted for subdivision (a) in the slayerstatute_core_disqualification clause above — not an independently distinct source, though it was itself fetched and confirmed identical across two independent requests. This clause states only what § 250(b) itself says about Prob. Code §§ 21110 and 673 (that they do not apply in this context); it does not independently research, quote, or describe what those two cross-referenced sections otherwise provide, and a reader wanting to understand California's general anti-lapse rule or power-of-appointment revocation rule should consult those sections directly rather than this clause.

JOINT TENANCY: SEVERANCE RATHER THAN AUTOMATIC SURVIVORSHIP
Joint tenancy property is addressed by its own statute, separate from § 250. Prob. Code § 251 provides that a joint tenant who feloniously and intentionally kills another joint tenant — rather than being outright disqualified from the whole property — effects a severance of the deceased joint tenant's interest, so that the deceased joint tenant's share passes as that decedent's own property (through their will, trust, or intestate succession, subject to the ordinary rules, including § 250 itself if the killer would otherwise take a share of it), and the killer acquires no right to the property by survivorship. The statute is not limited to real property joint tenancies: it expressly applies to joint tenancies in real and personal property, joint and multiple-party financial institution accounts, and any other form of coownership carrying survivorship incidents.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A joint tenant who feloniously and intentionally kills another joint tenant thereby effects a severance of the interest of the decedent so that the share of the decedent passes as the decedent’s property and the killer has no rights by survivorship. This section applies to joint tenancies in real and personal property, joint and multiple-party accounts in financial institutions, and any other form of coownership with survivorship incidents."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 251, California Probate Code, slayer statute's joint tenancy severance rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=251.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section, Prob. Code § 251, fetched twice independently (two distinct User-Agent strings) with identical results both times, and is a source independent of §§ 250, 253, and 254 quoted in the other clauses of this document. The statute's text does not itself spell out every downstream consequence of the severance — for example, exactly how the severed share is then divided among surviving co-tenants or distributed through the decedent's estate — and this clause does not go beyond what § 251 states to resolve that.

HOW A "FELONIOUS AND INTENTIONAL KILLING" IS ESTABLISHED
California's slayer statute does not require a criminal conviction before its disqualification rules can operate. Prob. Code § 254(a) makes a final judgment of conviction of felonious and intentional killing conclusive for purposes of Part 7 (the slayer-statute part). But § 254(b) goes further: in the absence of a final conviction — for example, where no criminal charges were ever filed, charges were dismissed, or the person was acquitted — a court (typically the probate court handling the estate, trust, or property dispute) may still determine by a preponderance of the evidence, the ordinary civil standard, whether the killing was felonious and intentional for purposes of the statute. That is a lower standard than the "beyond a reasonable doubt" standard used in a criminal trial. The statute places the burden of proof on whoever is asserting that the killing was felonious and intentional — that is, on the party seeking to disqualify the alleged killer, not on the alleged killer to disprove it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A final judgment of conviction of felonious and intentional killing is conclusive for purposes of this part. (b) In the absence of a final judgment of conviction of felonious and intentional killing, the court may determine by a preponderance of evidence whether the killing was felonious and intentional for purposes of this part. The burden of proof is on the party seeking to establish that the killing was felonious and intentional for the purposes of this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 254(a)-(b), California Probate Code, how a felonious and intentional killing is established for slayer-statute purposes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=254.)
  Known gap: Prob. Code § 254 is the identical statutory section already quoted elsewhere in this corpus, in the lifeinsbene_slayer_statute clause of the Life Insurance Beneficiary Designation Information Sheet, for the narrower life-insurance context; it is not an independent statutory source from that clause, though this document re-verifies it separately here (fetched twice independently, both times against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov with different User-Agent strings, with identical results) because the § 254 conviction-or-preponderance standard applies identically across every category the slayer statute reaches — wills, trusts, intestate succession, joint tenancy, and the other categories described in this document's other clauses — not only life insurance. This clause does not determine, and is not evidence toward, whether any actual killing occurred or was felonious and intentional in any particular case.

THE RESIDUAL RULE FOR OTHER PROPERTY A KILLER MIGHT ACQUIRE
The categories in § 250 (wills, trusts, intestate succession, quasi-community property, Division 5 nonprobate transfers, and Division 6 Part 3 family-protection property), § 251 (joint tenancy), and § 252 (a named beneficiary of a bond, life insurance policy, or other contractual arrangement — already addressed elsewhere in this corpus) do not exhaust every way a killer might acquire property, an interest, or a benefit as a result of a killing. Prob. Code § 253 supplies a residual rule for whatever is left over: in any case not described in § 250, § 251, or § 252 in which one person feloniously and intentionally kills another, any acquisition of property, interest, or benefit by the killer as a result of the killing is to be treated in accordance with the principles of Part 7 — that is, the same disqualification-and-predecease principles reflected in §§ 250–252, extended by analogy to the acquisition at hand.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In any case not described in Section 250, 251, or 252 in which one person feloniously and intentionally kills another, any acquisition of property, interest, or benefit by the killer as a result of the killing of the decedent shall be treated in accordance with the principles of this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 253, California Probate Code, slayer statute's residual rule for property not otherwise addressed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=253.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section, Prob. Code § 253, fetched and independently confirmed twice (two distinct User-Agent strings, identical results). Section 253's own text names § 252 as one of the three specifically-addressed categories it does not duplicate; § 252 is the life-insurance-beneficiary provision already covered by this corpus's separate lifeinsbene_slayer_statute clause, which is why this document does not separately quote or restate § 252 here. Because § 253 is a deliberately open-ended catch-all, the statute's text does not itself specify how its "principles of this part" apply to any particular kind of property or benefit not otherwise enumerated; that application is necessarily case-specific and left to the courts, and this clause does not resolve it for any actual situation.

CERTIFICATION AND SIGNATURE
I, Jordan Lee, certify that I have read this information sheet describing California's slayer statute, Probate Code §§ 250–254, that it states generally applicable California law rather than a conclusion about any actual person's conduct in connection with the estate of Pat Morgan, and that whether a specific killing was "felonious and intentional" within the meaning of these statutes is a determination for a court — established either by a final criminal conviction or, in the absence of one, by a civil finding made by a preponderance of the evidence, as Prob. Code § 254 describes — and is not something this information sheet determines, and not something it advises Jordan Lee on.

Executed on September 2, 2026 at Sacramento, California.
